title: Kettle or bulb: which costs more?
hook: The kettle says 2000 W, the bulb 60 W. So the kettle always costs more to run. Right?

knows: appliance labels give a power in watts
doesNotKnow: the difference between power (a rate) and energy (an amount)

misconception: The higher-wattage appliance always uses more energy and costs more to run.
objective: The learner can explain that power is how fast energy flows and the bill counts energy, power x time: a 60 W bulb on for 2 h (0.12 kWh) uses more than a 2000 W kettle for 3 min (0.10 kWh).

claims.text: Energy used = power x time; 1 kWh is 1 kW for 1 hour, or 3.6 million joules.
claims.source: E = P t; 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6e6 J. BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure, 9th ed.), table 8 (non-SI units accepted for use).

claims.text: A 2000 W kettle for 3 minutes uses 0.10 kWh; a 60 W bulb for 2 hours uses 0.12 kWh.
claims.source: 2 kW x 0.05 h = 0.10 kWh; 0.06 kW x 2 h = 0.12 kWh. The stage computes (P / 1000) x (minutes / 60) for the bulb 0.5-3 h and kettle 1-6 min; checked in node.

claims.text: Each minute of the kettle is 0.033 kWh and each minute of the bulb is 0.001 kWh; these are the slices of the bars.
claims.source: 2 kW x 1/60 h = 0.0333 kWh; 0.06 kW x 1/60 h = 0.001 kWh. The stage draws the kettle's lines every minute and the bulb's every 10 minutes (labelled).

claims.text: The lesson assumes each appliance draws its label power steadily for the whole run.
claims.source: Stated idealisation (reveal). Real kettles switch off at the boil and draw slightly below nameplate as the element heats; nameplate power is a rated value (IEC 60335-1, rated power input).

recall.question: A 1000 W heater runs for 6 minutes; a 10 W phone charger runs for 12 hours. Which uses more energy?
recall.why: Energy is power x time: heater 1 kW x 0.1 h = 0.10 kWh; charger 0.01 kW x 12 h = 0.12 kWh.
